newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan tea output seen at 300 mln kg in few years.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan tea output seen at 300 mln kg in few years.

text.p: Kenya's total tea production is likely to rise to 300 million kg by 2000, making the East African nation by far the world's biggest tea exporter, a leading tea broker said.
Norman Wilson, managing director of Africa Tea Brokers Ltd, said despite the huge drop expected in the 1997 crop after severe drought, the potential for Kenya's tea industry remained great.

"The drought has taken its toll, and the likelihood of a crop recovery in 1997 is very, very remote. I really don't think production will be more than 219 to 220 million kg for 1997 (versus 257 million kg last year)," Wilson said.

"The general long-term view for the development of the Kenyan tea industry is very, very good because of the advantages we have here in Kenya. The climate is very good, the altitude...is very good and the inherent soil quality is very good.
"Kenya has the capacity by the turn of the century...of producing at least 300 million kg. That will make it by far the biggest exporter in the world," Wilson said in an interview.
He said Kenya's biggest competitor on the export market, Sri Lanka, had overtaken Kenya this year as an exporter, but had no chances of increasing production the way Kenya did.
India, the world's biggest tea producer, had increasing problems supplying its domestic market, which opened up even more potential for Kenya, Wilson said.

"In a few years time India might have to import tea -- which is a very interesting factor for a country like Kenya. The constraining factor in all this is that India hasn't got the land available to grow more tea," Wilson said.
"In Kenya there is still land available for (new) planting in the commercial sector, while the prospect of growth in Sri Lanka is low. They are very close to capacity," he added.
Sri Lanka and Kenya both produced about 257 million kg in 1996, of which Kenya exported 243 million and Sri Lanka 242 million, according to Wilson.
India consumes most of its crop, leaving only 25 percent for export, or some 220 million kg a year. India's population rose by 2.5 percent while domestuc consumption rose by 3.0 percent.
Wilson said any recovery in Kenya's 1997 crop would need a miracle of favourable rains in the second half of the year followed by medium-warm weather conditions, which was very unlikely.
The biggest buyers of Kenyan tea are Britain, Pakistan, Egypt and Sudan.
Tea is the biggest revenue earner in Kenya, generating some $350 million in export earnings in 1996, or about 20 percent of total revenues.
